::: {.callout-important}
## Overall finding

The 15-week sequence has a **coherent conceptual spine, strong scaffolding, and
healthy executable materials**. It is ready for structured colleague review.

The audit's principal workload concern has now been addressed through an
approved [student workload guide](weeks/workload-guide.qmd): one guided main
lab workflow, 4-6 core exercises, selected AI audits, and explicit guided and
extension material. The course is **not yet ready to freeze its calendar**
because assessment displacement and exact calendar dates remain unresolved.
:::

Audit completed: **22 July 2026**

## Scope And Method

This audit reviewed:

- the syllabus, AI policy, assessment markers, and two project specifications;
- all 15 week pages and their 30 planned 75-minute meetings;
- all 15 slide decks, 31 labs, 15 exercise sets, and weekly indexes;
- 21 MATLAB and 30 R scripts;
- the transition from MATLAB to R and the prerequisite chain among weeks;
- the relationship between weekly work, quizzes, the semester examination,
  projects, and the final examination;
- internal links, navigation, document parsing, slide density, local code
  execution, GitHub validation, and GitHub Pages publication.

The audit does not decide the deferred quiz formats, examination architecture,
or project dates. The workload model recommended below was approved after the
audit; the remaining recommendations are proposals, not approved policy.

## Executive Assessment

| Area | Finding | Judgment |
|---|---|---|
| Conceptual progression | MATLAB foundations lead to R data work, reusable workflows, models, and final evidence reconciliation | Strong |
| Beginner scaffolding | Supplied data, small scripts, explicit checks, repeated datasets, and templates reduce blank-page work | Strong |
| Validation culture | Row counts, residuals, baselines, identifiers, tests, sensitivity, and clean runs recur meaningfully | Strong |
| AI integration | Activities progress from code defects to question drift, statistical claims, automation, and communication | Strong but must not become a second weekly assignment |
| Workload clarity | The full resource bank is now separated into core, guided, and extension work | Resolved through the [student workload guide](weeks/workload-guide.qmd) |
| Assessment-week feasibility | Only Quiz 1 has time explicitly reserved; Weeks 6, 8, 9, and 13 retain full plans beside assessments | Calendar-critical |
| Project sequencing | Preview, group release, checkpoint, validation, and completion stages now follow prerequisite instruction | Resolved through the [project milestone map](projects/project-milestones.qmd); exact dates remain open |
| Software readiness | Required access, scaffolded use, and optional tools are explicit; live institutional systems still require verification | Matrix resolved; live check pending |
| Navigation and publication | Weekly pages, exercises, labs, slides, code, and projects are linked and publish correctly | Strong |

## The Coherent Course Spine

| Phase | Weeks | Progression |
|---|---:|---|
| MATLAB foundations | 1-2 | Arrays, scripts, plots, functions, control flow, and tests |
| MATLAB numerical work | 3-5 | Fitting, interpolation, numerical methods, visualization, symbolic work, and independent checks |
| R transition | 6 | Familiar programming ideas, data frames, missingness, `ggplot2`, and a supplied report scaffold |
| R data reasoning | 7-10 | Transformation, EDA, import, tidy structure, typed cleaning, relationships, and joins |
| Reusable R workflows | 11-12 | Readable pipelines, function contracts, vectorization, iteration, and visible failures |
| Modeling and synthesis | 13-15 | Model meaning, diagnostics, repeated models, sensitivity, validation evidence, and communication |

The sequence contains no major prerequisite reversal. In particular:

- file import is delayed until Week 9 so beginners can first learn R using
  built-in data;
- R functions precede typed iteration;
- one-model interpretation precedes many-model automation;
- final communication reuses familiar data and introduces no new model;
- repeated use of `airquality` in Weeks 7 and 12-15 reduces dataset-switching
  cost during the most abstract material.

| 7 | 15 | 31 | 2 | 9 | Coherent but needs core-versus-extension labels |
| 8 | 16 | 32 | 2 | 9 | Calendar-critical full EDA week plus semester examination |

| 10 | 17 | 34 | 2 | 10 | High breadth across strings, factors, date-times, and joins |

Across the course, there are **227 learning goals, 475 slide sections, 31 labs,
and 137 exercises**. The slide decks themselves are not overcrowded: every
slide stays within the current nine-nonblank-line density threshold. The issue
is cumulative selection, not slide layout.

## Principal Workload Finding

Every weekly plan schedules essentially all 150 contact minutes. That precision
is useful for planning, but beginners need time for software launch problems,
typing errors, questions, reruns, and recovery after an unsuccessful attempt.
There is no visible contingency budget.

The larger ambiguity is outside class. A reader cannot tell whether a normal
week requires:

- the complete main lab;
- the complete AI lab;
- every exercise;
- only the tasks embedded in the two meeting plans; or
- some instructor-selected subset.

That distinction is now made in the student workload guide. It bounds routine
website-based practice at approximately 90-120 minutes outside class in an
ordinary week, excluding separately announced project and examination work.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Adopted workload model

- The main lab supplies one **guided core workflow**; the instructor selects
  its checkpoints.
- The AI activity is embedded or assigned selectively, not automatically added
  as a second full lab.
- Each week identifies 4-6 **core exercises**; the remainder is guided or
  extension work.
- Core does not mean that every item is submitted. Blackboard or the instructor
  identifies any required upload.
- Assessment weeks receive a reduced selection when an assessment displaces
  class time.
- Routine website-based practice targets 90-120 minutes outside class in an
  ordinary week, excluding project and examination preparation.
:::

## Week-Specific Beginner Risks

### Weeks 1-5: MATLAB

- **Week 2** asks for functions, conditionals, logical indexing, `switch`,
  `for`, `while`, preallocation, vectorization, and tests. The conceptual core
  is functions, conditions, logical indexing, one loop pattern, and tests;
  `switch` and `while` can remain reference or extension material.
- **Week 4** is the broadest MATLAB week and has three labs. The ODE mini-lab
  should be identified as an alternate or extension unless additional contact
  time exists.
- **Week 5** is a coherent symbolic capstone, but student machines must have
  the required MATLAB symbolic capability before the week begins.
- Project 1 previously became visible only in Week 5 even though most required
  techniques are learned in Weeks 1-4. The approved milestone map now previews
  it in Week 3 and releases the group package in Week 4 without fixing the final
  due date.

### Weeks 6-10: R transition and data

- **Week 6** carries the largest software transition: R objects, data frames,
  missing values, selection, checks, `ggplot2`, and rendering a supplied report.
  The current text correctly avoids requiring students to author Quarto, but a
  pre-class software check is essential.
- **Week 8** cannot simultaneously retain two complete EDA meetings and use
  substantial in-class time for the semester examination. The examination
  location and duration must be resolved before this week is considered
  feasible.
- **Week 9** combines import contracts and reshaping effectively, but Quiz 3
  has no reserved time in either meeting.
- **Week 10** is pedagogically coherent but unusually broad. Join contracts and
  observation preservation should remain the central outcome; the separate
  string, factor, and date-time tools can be scaffolded around that purpose.

### Weeks 11-15: reusable workflows, models, and projects

- **Week 11** benefits from the MATLAB function experience, but expected-error
  testing with `tryCatch` is a candidate for scaffolded recognition rather than
  independent mastery.
- **Week 12** compares `lapply`, `vapply`, and a preallocated loop while also
  introducing safe failure records and Project 2. This is coherent but dense;
  the Project 2 orientation should not consume the only practice time for
  iteration.
- **Week 13** is a large first modeling week—formula meaning, coefficients,
  baseline error, R-squared, diagnostics, an additive model, and Quiz 4. Its
  feasibility depends on quiz delivery and students' retained statistical
  background.
- **Week 14** is appropriately constrained to one formula and familiar data.
  Students should modify and interpret a supplied many-model scaffold rather
  than be expected to construct the entire abstraction from a blank file.
- **Week 15** should function primarily as a project workshop and release
  rehearsal. Its 47-slide deck is a reference bank across two meetings, not a
  signal that every slide, lab part, and exercise is new required work.

## Assessment And Calendar Coherence

The working placements remain internally consistent with the syllabus: quizzes
in Weeks 3, 6, 9, and 13; the semester examination in Week 8; Project 2 around
Week 15. However, only Week 3 reserves quiz time in its meeting plan.

Before final calendar approval, the course needs one table recording:

- whether each quiz is in class, in Blackboard outside class, or completed in
  another scheduled period;
- how many teaching minutes it displaces;
- whether the Week 8 examination replaces one or both meetings;
- exact dates for the approved Project 1 preview, release, readiness, and
  completion gates;
- exact dates for the approved Project 2 training release, frozen-plan,
  validation release, and completion gates;
- where cumulative final-examination review occurs.

The assessment formats may remain deferred, but the amount of displaced
teaching time cannot remain unknown when judging beginner workload.

## Project Workload

Both projects are unusually well scaffolded: students receive data, starters,
result schemas, Word templates, and fixed checks. That makes ambitious work
possible for groups with limited programming experience.

The audit originally identified timing rather than architecture as the
remaining concern:

- Project 1 has 12 visible starter `TODO` markers and previously became visible
  only in Week 5.
- Project 2 has 14 visible starter `TODO` markers, depends on modeling taught in
  Weeks 13-14, and completes around Week 15.
- Each project is worth 10%, so required report length, figure count, and
  expected group effort should be bounded explicitly.

The recommended pattern has now been approved:

| Project | Earlier orientation | Technical milestone | Completion window |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project 1 | Preview in Week 3 | Group package in Week 4; readiness checkpoint in Week 5 | Opens after Week 5; exact deadline set later with Quiz 2 |
| Project 2 | Preview in Weeks 9-10 | Training release in Week 12; frozen plan after Week 13; common validation release in Week 14 | Week 15; exact deadline set later |

The [student-facing milestone map](projects/project-milestones.qmd) and
instructor Blackboard release map make the order explicit without deciding
calendar dates or assessment formats.

## AI Activity Coherence

The AI strand is cumulative rather than decorative:

1. syntax, dimensions, and plotting defects;
2. function and boundary failures;
3. overfitting and numerical evidence;
4. symbolic assumptions;
5. causal plot language;
6. question drift and lost data meaning;
7. partial joins and behavior-changing refactors;
8. erased batch failures;
9. model interpretation and ranking;
10. cross-artifact and conclusion claims.

The content is preserved. Its adopted workload label now treats AI audits as
part of the core computational question or as selected practice, not
automatically as an additional full weekly deliverable.

## Terminology And Recovery

The course intentionally repeats useful words—contract, baseline, residual,
diagnostic, sensitivity, observation unit, and reproducibility—but there is no
student glossary or phase-level recovery page.

Two low-cost supports would materially help beginners:

- a one-page evolving glossary with a short example for each recurring term;
- a “minimum knowledge before the next phase” checklist after Weeks 5, 10, and
  12, with links to one recovery script and one recovery exercise.

These supports matter because missing Week 6, 9, 11, or 13 creates a strong
downstream dependency.

## Software And Access

This audit finding is now resolved at the policy and publication level. The
[student software matrix](resources/software-requirements.qmd) distinguishes:

- reliable MATLAB and R access from mandatory personal installation;
- the Week 5 Symbolic Math Toolbox dependency;
- one supported R editor and the six packages actually used by the course;
- Quarto as a required, scaffolded Week 6 activity rather than a project-report
  format;
- Word/Google Docs-compatible editing, PDF export, Blackboard, and ZIP handling
  as operational requirements; and
- Git/GitHub and paid generative-AI accounts as optional.

The two runnable setup scripts test the real computational workflow. The
[instructor readiness checklist](resources/instructor-setup-checklist.qmd)
separates this approved contract from the still-unverified claim that a
particular laboratory, license route, or Blackboard configuration provides it.

## Technical And Publication QA

At the audit point:

- all 30 R scripts and the Week 6 report code pass the complete R harness;
- all executable MATLAB scripts pass the local MATLAB harness, including
  expected-failure classification for the intentionally weak AI example;
- GitHub's R validation workflow passes on the Week 15 commit;
- the GitHub Pages workflow renders and deploys the Week 15 commit;
- every QMD file parses successfully with Pandoc;
- all relative Markdown links resolve locally;
- all weekly scripts, labs, and slide decks appear in their indexes;
- every slide deck remains within the nine-nonblank-line density threshold;
- the Week 15 public page returns HTTP 200.

GitHub validates R automatically; MATLAB remains a local licensed-runtime
check. External documentation links and rendered visual accessibility should be
rechecked shortly before the teaching term.

## Recommended Decision Order

1. **Completed: approve a workload-label model:** core, guided, and extension
   materials are now identified in the student workload guide.
2. **Resolve assessment displacement:** especially Week 8 and quizzes in Weeks
   6, 9, and 13.
3. **Completed: set project milestones:** preview, release, frozen plan,
   validation, and completion are now fixed relative to course weeks.
4. **Completed: publish the student software matrix;** now run and record the
   separate live lab-machine and Blackboard check.
5. **Add glossary and recovery checkpoints** at the three phase boundaries.
6. **Build an assessment blueprint** after quiz and examination formats are
   chosen, including a place for cumulative final-examination review.
7. **Then revise individual meeting plans**, preserving the coherent spine and
   using the approved labels to select what fits the available time.

## Audit Boundary

This audit recommends no deletion of the resource bank and does not change
approved assessment policy. Its workload recommendation has been implemented;
its project milestone and software-matrix recommendations have also been
implemented. The assessment calendar, exact project dates, live institutional
setup verification, and recovery supports remain to be resolved.
